name: Bahmani and Deccan sultanates
summary: The Bahmani Sultanate of the Deccan (1347–1527) and the five sultanates that followed it (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda, Bidar, Berar); they defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565) and were conquered by the Mughals by 1687.

location.value: The Deccan plateau, between the Krishna River and the Vindhya Range; the Bijapur sultanate straddled the Western Ghats.

terrain.value: A high, dry plateau with river valleys (Krishna, Godavari).

climate.value: Hot and dry, with seasonal monsoon rains.

disasters.value: A great famine in 1630–32 killed many in the Deccan.

population.value: The article gives no population estimate.

urbanisation.value: Capitals such as Gulbarga, Bidar, Bijapur, Golconda/Hyderabad and Ahmadnagar.

disease.value: Famines and epidemics; the Deccan famine of 1630–32 killed millions.

migration.value: Persian, Turkish and African (Habshi) soldiers and officials.

economicBase.value: Mainly farming and trade. Bidar was known for Bidriware metalwork. The page does not mention Golconda's diamonds or textiles.

tradeRoutes.value: Ports on both coasts linked the Deccan to Persia, Arabia and Southeast Asia.

wealth.value: Golconda’s diamonds are not mentioned in the article read.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold and silver coins, and land revenue.

inequality.value: Rulers and military elites above farmers and herders.

governmentType.value: Muslim sultanates whose courts the article calls Persianate.

keyRulers.value: Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur (1580–1627), Quli Qutb Shah, founder of Golconda (1512–43), and Malik Ambar, prime minister of Ahmadnagar. Mahmud Gawan is not named on this page.

succession.value: Bahmani dynasty, then five dynasties (Nizam Shahi, Adil Shahi, Qutb Shahi, Barid Shahi, Imad Shahi).

institutions.value: Persian-style administration; Hindu officials ran revenue collection.

stability.value: Frequent wars between the sultanates and with Vijayanagara.

eliteConflict.value: Deccanis (local-born nobles) competed with foreign-born nobles at court.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry, war elephants and artillery, including the huge Malik-i-Maidan cannon at Bijapur.

majorWars.value: Battle of Talikota (1565): the sultanates allied against Vijayanagara, and the city was destroyed.

territoryChange.value: Berar was taken from Ahmadnagar by the Mughals in 1596.

alliancesRivals.value: Allied against Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565); fought the Mughals and the Portuguese.

inventions.value: No major inventions; known for metalwork (bidri ware).

scienceEducation.value: Mahmud Gawan’s madrasa at Bidar (1472) taught science and Islamic studies.

openness.value: Open to Persian, Turkish and African migrants and to trade.

communicationTransport.value: Caravan roads and ports such as Goa (before 1510) and Machilipatnam.

religion.value: Muslim rulers. Ahmadnagar made Shia Islam its state religion in 1538; Bijapur moved strongly towards Sunni Islam. Rulers were tolerant of Hindus, who worked in administration. The page gives no population shares.

languageWriting.value: Persian at court; Dakhni (early Urdu), Telugu, Kannada and Marathi.

artsArchitecture.value: Gol Gumbaz, Charminar, Golconda Fort and Deccani painting.

socialStructure.value: Deccani and foreign-born Muslim nobles, Habshi (African) commanders, Hindu officials and peasants.

sharedIdentity.value: A distinct Deccani Persian culture, with its own Urdu-Dakhni language.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; biryani cooking traditions grew at the Golconda court.

neighbours.value: Vijayanagara, the Mughals, Portuguese Goa, the Marathas.

ideasReligions.value: Persianate culture and Sufism were influential, alongside Hindu traditions.

colonisation.value: None; the Portuguese held coastal forts.

riseSignals.value: The sultanates emerged after the Bahmani Sultanate disintegrated; Ahmadnagar declared independence in 1490.

peakPeriod.value: The page names no peak. It shows four sultanates defeating Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565) and Ibrahim Adil Shah II's patronage of the arts (1580–1627).

declineSignals.value: Mughal campaigns took Ahmadnagar (1636), Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).

outcome.value: Conquered by the Mughals: Ahmadnagar (1633–1636), Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
